name: Uchinathar (Ujjivanathar) Temple, Tirukkarkudi
deity: Shiva as Uchinathar (Ujjivanathar), with the goddess Anjanakshi
period: Ancient hill-top Shaiva shrine sung in the Tevaram (7th century); rock-set temple with Chola-era inscriptions from 941 CE
dynasty: Early Chola (inscriptions of Parantaka I, Uttama Chola and Sembiyan Mahadevi) and later patrons
summary: Uchinathar crowns the rocky hill of Tirukkarkudi at Uyyakondan Tirumalai, the Tevaram shrine where tradition says the young sage Markandeya took refuge in the Lord and was granted lasting youth.

sections.history: On a small hill about five kilometres west of Tiruchirappalli stands the shrine the Tevaram hymns call Tirukkarkudi, the sacred settlement on the rock. In later ages the hill took the name Uyyakondan Tirumalai from the nearby Uyyakondan channel, believed to have been cut in the time of the Chola kings in the ninth century, and it is still known also as Karkudimalai. The Nayanmars sang of the shrine, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The earliest inscriptions are cut on the pillars of the inner enclosure: one is dated to the thirty-fourth regnal year of Parantaka I, which is 941 CE, and later records belong to the reigns of Uttama Chola and the queen Sembiyan Mahadevi. The original complex is believed to be a work of the Cholas, and it has been tended in worship ever since.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered through an east-facing gopuram of five tiers at the foot of the hill, from where a long flight of steps cut into the living rock climbs to the main complex; sources count sixty-five steps in one place and a hundred in another. After the entrance, to the left, lies the temple tank known as the Gnana Vavi, the well of wisdom. The sanctum, set high on the hill, holds Shiva as the linga of Uchinathar, also called Ujjivanathar, the Lord who gives life. The goddess is honoured as Anjanakshi, the mother whose eyes are dark as kohl, and she is known also by the names Balambikai and Neelanedunkanni.
sections.legends: The legend of Tirukkarkudi belongs to the sage Markandeya. Tradition tells that, devoted to the Lord on this hill, he took refuge in him and embraced the linga, and that Ujjivanathar granted him a life without ending: he remained for ever the youth of sixteen, a Chiranjeevi. From this the shrine is held to bestow long life and prosperity on those who live in its shadow. The sages Upamanyu and Karan are remembered among the worshippers of this hill, and so is the poet-saint Arunagirinathar. The very name Ujjivanathar keeps the meaning of the story: the Lord by whom life is saved and made whole.
sections.festivals: The Panguni festival, the Brahmotsavam of March and April, is the most prominent day of the temple's year, when the deities are taken in procession around the hill. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are kept with devotion, as at all festivals dedicated to Shiva. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: A visit to Tirukkarkudi begins with a climb, and the climb is part of the offering. Pass beneath the five-tiered gopuram, ascend the rock-cut steps at an easy pace, and pause at the Gnana Vavi before entering the sanctum of Uchinathar. Pray then to Anjanakshi, and remember Markandeya, whose story the hill still tells to those who ask for a long and good life. Though the temple lies within reach of the city, the height and the stone give it the stillness of a hermitage on a hill.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the foot of the steps, so wear shoes that are easy to remove and carry water for the climb.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer areas of the temple but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Uyyakondan Tirumalai lies on the Tiruchirappalli–Vayalur road, on the western outskirts of Tiruchirappalli, about 5 km from the city. City buses and autorickshaws serve the hill, and Tiruchirappalli Junction is the main railway station. The city's airport is the nearest for air travellers. Do not confuse this shrine with the other Uchinathar temple, at Sivapuri, which is a separate site.
